1.0.s.en: 1. The piety and wealth of Job

1.0.0.en: 1 There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil. 2 And there were born unto him seven sons and three daughters. 3 His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east.

1.0.1.en: "There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job;

1.0.2.en: and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil" [1].

1.0.3.en: Many of the Fathers see that the book opens with a great praise of him in the words, "There was a man." As Origen says, many are called human beings, yet they behave like beasts of prey, or stupid animals, or reptiles, or birds, and not as men, according to how God, the Lover of mankind, created them.

1.0.4.en: * This name "man" we do not define as those who are outside define it, but as the Holy Bible defines it. A human being is not everyone who has the hands and feet of a man, nor merely one who is rational, but one who practices godliness and virtue with courage.

1.0.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * Many call themselves "men" (human beings), but they are not truly so. Some live with the conduct of beasts, while others live with the conduct of reptiles, spewing out their wrath like wild beasts. Therefore David himself says, "Nevertheless man being in honour abideth not: he is like the beasts" (Ps 49:12)...

1.0.6.en: But surely the word "man" is used of one who bears the image of God (Gen 1:27), who guards his dignity in a fitting manner, and sets the choice between good and evil, and gives his glory to his creation, which rejoices in him and finds its delight in him (Ps 104:31).

1.0.7.en: So "there was a man in the land of Uz." The region was a desolate wilderness, yet in it was planted... Job was a treasure lacking nothing. He was full of the grapes of the planted vintage. He was perfect (true), like the creation of the true God, for he used his virtues for the sake of the truth without hypocrisy, fulfilling the commandments of God... He worshipped God as God wishes.

1.0.8.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The sons of Edom dwelt in "Uz" in the days of Jeremiah the prophet (Lam 4:21). It is believed that it lay between Damascus and Edom, in the Syrian desert. Some believe that it is Hauran. It lies between Palestine and Arabia, north-east of the river Euphrates, on the caravan route between Egypt and Babylon. Tradition holds that Haran is Job's homeland, east of the Sea of Galilee. It was an exceedingly fertile region, and it contained about 300 small cities.

1.0.9.en: Perhaps Uz was not far from Ur of the Chaldees, from which Abraham was called. If God called Abraham to raise up from his seed a chosen people, He still had a remnant that bore witness to Him among the Gentiles. And God's plan for humanity is fulfilled when we share with St. John in enjoying this sight: "A great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne" (Rev 7:9).

1.0.10.en: God brought Abraham out of that corrupt land, where God calls His chosen ones to withdraw from evil. And He permitted Job to remain, that he might be a witness to His divine light in the midst of the thick darkness, like the stars in the darkness of the night.

1.0.11.en: * To make known the worth of his virtue, we are told where the holy man dwelt, for who does not know that Uz is a Gentile land? The Gentile world was under the authority of the evil one, and accordingly its eyes were closed to the knowledge of its Creator. So let us be told where he dwelt, for in this there is praise of him. He was a good man dwelling among wicked people. It is no great praise to be good in the company of the good; but to be good while dwelling in the midst of the wicked is a testimony that cannot be measured...

1.0.12.en: For it is said, "And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: for that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds" (2 Pet 2:7-8)...

1.0.13.en: And so Paul says to his disciples, "In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world" (Phil 2:15).

1.0.14.en: And it was said to the angel of the church of Pergamos, "I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith" (Rev 2:13).

1.0.15.en: So the Church was praised by the voice of the Bridegroom, who says in the Song of Songs, "As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters" (Song 2:2)...

1.0.16.en: Rightly it is said of him that he "eschewed evil," for it is written, "Depart from evil, and do good" (Ps 37:27). For truly, good works are not acceptable to God if in His eyes they are stained by being mixed with evil works, as it was said by Solomon, [He who sins in one matter destroys much good] (cf. Eccl 9:18). James bears witness to this, saying, "For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all" (Jas 2:10). Paul says, "A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (1 Cor 5:6).

1.0.17.en: It was fitting, then, to point out how he eschewed evil works, in order to show how the blessed Job was without blemish and steadfast in his good works.

1.0.19.en: The word of God bears witness to Job's perfection: "And that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." 1. Perfect: this is a relative perfection, and it does not mean that he was without sin, but that he seeks perfection and strives to attain it as far as he is able.

1.0.20.en: * The Apostle speaks of himself as being perfect and not perfect. He counts himself not perfect, looking at how much righteousness he still lacks, yet he is perfect in that he is not ashamed to confess his imperfection and that he presses on to attain perfection.

1.0.21.en: St. Augustine * There are two forms of perfection, an ordinary form and a heavenly one. One is acquired here, the other hereafter. One is according to human capacities, the other belongs to the perfection of the world to come; but God is just through all, wise above all, perfect in all.

1.0.22.en: St. Ambrose 1. Upright: in his dealings with God and men, that is, he bears a spirit of simplicity without twisting or inward deviation. What he practices reveals what is in his heart, without malice. He is upright in his conduct, scrutinizing his thoughts, words and actions, faithful in his time and appointments and in the talents given to him. 2. Godly: he worships God with a godly spirit, not in dry formalities without spirit. He strives to fulfil the will of God; in other words, his conduct is in harmony with his worship of God; he fears God lest he offend against His majesty and love. 3. Eschewing evil: the fear of the Lord is a wall surrounding him, so that he does not allow evil to creep into his thought, or his heart, or his conduct.

1.0.23.en: * It is said that he was upright, "without blemish," and it does not say "without sin"... Why was he without blemish? Because he was upright.

1.0.24.en: He was "true" because men are liars (Ps 62:9).

1.0.25.en: He was "true," not in words only but in deeds also. By this he is "a man of truth." For "Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole of man" (Eccl 12:13). Job was zealous for pure conduct; therefore the text says that he was "godly and true," and it brought out the cause of all his virtues, that he feared God... The knowledge of God is made manifest in a person's life, and becomes a guardian of life...

1.0.26.en: It does not say, "He did not commit evil," but "he eschewed evil"... In another passage: "Lest I be full, and deny, and say, Who is the LORD?" (Prov 30:9). You see that unless a man is careful, satiety is the foundation of deception. But this was not Job's condition.

1.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "And there were born unto him seven sons and three daughters" [2].

1.1.1.en: With the multitude of his offspring, righteous Job was not preoccupied with his possessions, in order to give a great inheritance to each son or daughter of his; rather, what occupied him was giving them a vast inheritance of prayers, praises, spiritual sacrifices and burnt offerings as a support for them.

1.1.2.en: Origen sees in the sons and daughters a symbol of the work of the Holy Spirit in the life of the believer, in whom He begets or bears, through his soul as through his body, holy spiritual fruits for the Lord. For the godly man, like Job, has the Spirit of God working in him, so the soul is in harmony with the body, and he is wholly under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us, in detail and at length, symbolic interpretations of the seven sons and the three daughters, of which we quote very little.

1.1.3.en: * What does the number 7 present to us other than the summit of perfection...? The seven sons represent the order of the preachers, and the three daughters may point to the three classes of believers in the life of the Church... pastors, virgins and the married.

1.1.4.en: Seven sons are born to us when we conceive by good intention, and the seven virtues of the Holy Spirit are born in us. The prophet gave attention to this spiritual offspring in particular when the Holy Spirit makes the mind fruitful, in these words: [And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord, and shall fill him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord] (cf. Isa 11:2-3). So when wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, godliness and the fear of the Lord are begotten in each of us at the coming of the Holy Spirit, an offspring has been born in the mind, which preserves the lineage of our heavenly honor in life, where it is allied all the more with eternal love.

1.1.5.en: Surely the seven sons in us have three sisters, since each of them (the sons) works with maturity (manliness) with virtuous inclinations, and so is united with faith, hope and love. For the number 7 will not reach the perfection of the number 10 unless they do everything in faith, hope and love.

1.1.7.en: After speaking of his inward wealth, that of the soul, in that he had seven sons, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, together with three daughters, that is, faith, hope and love, he spoke of his bodily wealth. For the children point to the wealth of the Spirit, and the animals point to the wealth of the body that is sanctified in the Lord. So he suffers neither spiritual want nor bodily want, since the Creator of soul and body satisfies his whole being.

1.1.8.en: "His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke (pair) of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household;

1.2.0.en: so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east" [3].

1.2.1.en: With his enormous wealth he was marked by righteousness. The sheep are mentioned first because they were necessary for families: "The lambs are for thy clothing... goats' milk enough for thy food, for the food of thy household, and for the maintenance for thy maidens" (Prov 27:26-27). His servants were very many; all served him and his house.

1.2.2.en: Among the customs that still remain among shepherds and Bedouin societies is that a person's riches and wealth are estimated not by his land or his houses, but by the livestock he owns. Abraham was very rich in his flocks (Gen 13:2). Lot also had his flocks (Gen 13:5). So Job's wealth is estimated by the number of animals he owns. He mentioned the female donkeys (she asses) because their value was much greater than that of the males on account of the milk that was used for drinking.

1.2.3.en: Some see that Job's sheep and camels point to the union of the age of the Law with the age of grace. The seven thousand sheep point to the pasture of the Law, which becomes perfect through spiritual touches (the number thousand) in place of the letter; to this pasture are joined the three thousand camels, as the peoples of the Gentiles come to join the pasture of the spiritual Law, and all become one flock with one shepherd.

1.2.4.en: * Job was rich, but he did not spend his life in luxury without compassion (for others). His house was open to everyone in need, by his will that was full of love. He treated no one with injustice, but helped those who suffered injustice; he provided the necessary needs for widows and orphans. For these are the works of righteousness of the righteous rich man.

1.3.0.en: 4 And his sons went and feasted in their houses, every one his day; and sent and called for their three sisters to eat and to drink with them. 5 And it was so, when the days of their feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually.

1.3.1.en: "And his sons went and feasted in their houses, every one his day; and sent and called for their three sisters, to eat and to drink with them" [4].

1.3.2.en: A wonderful picture of a very rich man whom wealth and riches did not preoccupy, nor did they preoccupy his sons; rather all gather in a spirit of love and unity with good management, and they hold a feast in the house of each son in turn, with fellowship with the sisters! His sons held periodic feasts in a spirit of love and unity. Each son held the feast in his turn, gathering his brothers and sisters. The psalmist says, "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" (Ps 133:1).

1.3.3.en: The following is observed in these feasts: 1. They were held in houses, not in public places, perhaps so that the family would keep its holy character even at feasts and in the midst of joys. 2. The invitation of the sisters is an indication that the feasts were family feasts, and most probably limited to Job's family. 3. Job did not go to the feasts, not out of rigidity, for he seeks the joy and delight of his children as long as it is in the Lord; but his presence as an old man might have in it a kind of not giving the young people the freedom to be merry yet, even if it was in the Lord.

1.3.4.en: * Great wealth is usually a cause of disputes among brothers. What an inestimable praise of the upbringing of such a father! The wealth of the father and the peace of the brothers together were proclaimed, for while the wealth was divided among them, love was not divided, but filled the hearts of all!

1.3.6.en: "And it was so, when the days of their feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts.

1.4.1.en: Although Job did not take part in the feasts bodily, he took part spiritually in a spirit of tender fatherhood and love. He was zealous for the salvation of their souls, fearing lest they be defiled even in thought, and so be counted as blasphemers against the Holy One.

1.4.2.en: He feared lest one of them think in the depths of his heart, saying, "My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth" (Deut 8:17). Or, as the wise man says, "Lest I be full, and deny, and say, Who is the LORD?" (Prov 30:9).

1.4.3.en: Job was the priest of the family. He believed that he was unable to sanctify his children, and that this is the work of God; therefore he offered burnt offerings according to their number. He did this not only at the beginning of the feast, nor only at its end, but throughout all the days of the feast, and all the days of the year. "Thus did Job continually." Perhaps he offered a burnt sacrifice for the whole family every day, but in the days of the feasts he offered a burnt offering for each one, because sins, especially those of thought, find in feasts a suitable atmosphere to creep inside.

1.4.4.en: * If sins committed in ignorance are judged to be so grievous and need a sacrifice to atone for them, a truth to which Job bore witness by offering a sacrifice for his children, what then is to be said of those who commit sin knowingly, or those who in their silence yield to the sinful conduct of others?

1.4.5.en: St. Basil the Great * He offered his sacrifices for their hidden sins and their unconfessed faults. If Job took such care concerning hidden sins committed without knowledge, how much more, do you think, concerning manifest faults. Notice how he translates the words of the Apostle into action: "And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Eph 6:4), that is, a person takes care of his children. It is a practice of parental protection. Notice to what level of perfection he wished to lead them...

1.4.6.en: For manifest faults he could correct them, but what could he do about secret sins? Yet it was said to Moses, "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deut 29:29). At any rate, Job did not ignore even the secret faults in their relation to God, but obliged himself to correct the situation personally by a remedial means. For this means allowed him to strike at the faults and uproot them, and also to teach his children...

1.4.7.en: You see that he corrected not only their shortcomings in deeds, but also what concerns thoughts, practically fulfilling the words of Christ: "For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts... These are the things which defile a man" (Mt 15:19-20)... You see here a purification that is not Mosaic, nor by the Law, but in an apostolic manner, in that he seeks the purification of their thoughts daily, not only by advising them and giving them counsel, but also by protecting them and praying to God for them. This is not the work of a father only, but also of a priest, though we know that there was not yet a priest...

1.4.8.en: Some see that there were priests in those days also, such as Melchizedek, whom the people did not choose.

1.4.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * The very words of Scripture indicate that ignorance is a sin. This is the reason why Job offers burnt offerings for his sons, lest they had sinned unwittingly in thought.

1.4.10.en: St. Jerome * This statement attributed to Job shows very great godliness. For many people are accustomed to rise early for earthly occupations, and all they think about during the night is the means of amassing wealth or glory or honors, so they hasten to rise to carry out their thoughts in practice. The prophet expresses, in a song of lamentation, what must be said about these: "Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it" (Mic 2:1). But Job was not occupied with this; rather, at dawn he offered service to God, who makes the light shine... For the true sacrifice is the keeping of the Law and the practice of virtues (Sir 35:1-3). The words of Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews serve us in this as an example: "By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually... But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased" (Heb 13:15-16).

1.4.11.en: "For Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts" [5]. Job's uprightness is clear! He completes his righteousness toward goodness. He is a wise father and an experienced master, a tower (of the stars) marked by prudence, a good guide like one who holds an outer bridle to restrain the inner passions... David was not content to sing those words: "Who can understand his errors? Cleanse me from secret faults" (Ps 19:12), but he also put the commandment of the Gospel into practice. We say that Job walked according to the Law and grace, and according to the commandment of the Gospel: "...Which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it" (Lk 8:15). He did not take this lightly. John the Theologian wrote on this: "And shall assure our hearts before him. For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God" (1 Jn 3:19-21), and the Lord Himself says, "For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies: These are the things which defile a man: but to eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man" (Mt 15:19-20). Let us then be purified from these deeds. Let us seek fruit from our souls every day, for Job was "true and blameless," looking also to what is written: "Thus did Job continually" [5].

1.4.12.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Thus Job purified his children, for one who offers sacrifices for secret sins, how much more does he care about manifest sins?

1.4.13.en: * Job used a remedy even for the thoughts of his sons.

1.4.14.en: St. John Chrysostom * "And rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all" [5]. The saint knew that a feast is rarely held without transgression. He knew that the merriment of feasts must be purified by sacrifices. And the stains that the sons had committed in their persons during their feasts the father washed away by offering a sacrifice... for feasts are often accompanied by passions, and when the body is relaxed by pleasures the heart submits to vain joy. For it is written, "The people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play" (Ex 32:6).

1.4.16.en: Job was at ease about the conduct of his sons and daughters in their love for one another and their oneness of spirit and harmony together, and he was reassured about their behavior and words, but he did not know what was going on in their thoughts and hearts. He did not take the position of a judge, passing judgment on what was inside them, nor did he stand in negligence, considering himself not responsible for what was in their hearts; rather, in a love full of wisdom he had recourse to God by offering spiritual sacrifices and burnt offerings for each one of them. For He alone knows the hidden secrets, and is able to sanctify the depths.

1.4.17.en: * "Thus did Job continually" [5]. Job did not cease offering a perpetual sacrifice, just as our Savior offers a burnt offering for us without interruption. He shows His incarnation before the Father for our sake without ceasing. For His very incarnation is an offering for our cleansing; and while He shows Himself as a man He is an intercessor who washes away the impurities of man, offering through the mystery of His humanity a perpetual sacrifice...

1.4.18.en: Vain is the goodness we practice if it stops before the end of life, for it is vain for one who runs swiftly to stop before reaching the goal. Concerning this the rebuke was given: "Woe unto you that have lost patience!" (Sir 2:14). And so the Truth says to His chosen ones: "Ye are they which have continued with me in my temptations" (Lk 22:28)... So Moses ordered that the tail of the sacrifice be offered on the altar, meaning that every good work we begin we complete with perseverance to the end.

1.4.20.en: * In general, the commandments of all the saints urge us to this by example, just as Solomon used in Proverbs, saying, "Hear, ye children, the instruction of the Lord, and attend to know understanding. For I give you good doctrine, forsake ye not my law. For I was my father's son, tender and only beloved in the sight of my mother" (Prov 4:1-3). For the righteous father brings up his children well, as he strives to teach others by his upright and virtuous conduct. So that if opposition arises, he is not ashamed to hear this saying: "Thou... which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself?" (Rom 21:2), but rather he is like a faithful servant who is able to save himself and gain others. And as the grace entrusted to him is multiplied he can hear that saying: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord" (Mt 21:25).

1.5.0.en: 6 Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them. 7 And the LORD said unto Satan, Whence comest thou? Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it. 8 And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? 9 Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought? 10 Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land. 11 But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face. 12 And the LORD said unto Satan, Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand. So Satan went forth from the presence of the LORD.

1.5.1.en: "Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them" [6].

1.5.2.en: It is stated in the Jerusalem Targum, Targum Yerushalmi, that the two councils held in heaven, one was on Rosh ha-Shanah, and the second on Yom Kippur.

1.5.3.en: The angels, the sons of God, would gather together before God to offer Him the fitting praise for His love for the heavenly and the earthly beings, and to present also the prayers of the believers, and to await any mission they might fulfil, for they are servants for those who shall be heirs of salvation (Heb 1:14).

1.5.4.en: Satan, the proud deceiver, slipped in among them to complain against humanity, especially the believers, for in his envy he cannot bear to see an earthly man grow in the Spirit and take flight as on the wings of a dove to heaven.

1.5.5.en: All things are open before God; He has no need of angels to carry to Him the prayers of His believers, nor of Satan to disclose the corruption of some believer. But God, in His love for the heavenly beings, grants them the work of love, whether by presenting prayers or by fulfilling His mission. And in His justice He leaves Satan the freedom to complain against whomever he wishes. He hallows the freedom of will in rational creatures, whether at the level of the heavenly orders, or the spiritual powers of evil, or human beings.

1.5.6.en: We should not wonder at this, for in the vision of Zechariah the prophet, when he saw the Word of God Himself as a high priest bearing our sins like a filthy garment, Satan stood to resist him (Zech 3:1-2).

1.5.7.en: St. John Chrysostom asks us not to be astonished that the rebel stands among the angels, for what the book presents is in human form so that we may understand the situation with our human mind.

1.5.8.en: * The angels came, according to the text, and Satan came with them, as he was going about the earth and walking up and down under heaven. What do we understand from this? That the earth is full of demons and angels, and all are under the authority of the power of God, and that the angels stand before God, where they receive orders from Him. And Satan cannot do anything he pleases unless he obtains permission from above... The saying, "Satan came also among them" [6], means only that he too cannot do anything without God's permission.

1.5.9.en: * What does this expression mean? He is with them in the world, for just as deceitful men and good men are mingled together, so are angels and demons.

1.5.10.en: St. John Chrysostom Perhaps the utmost a man desires is to enjoy heavenly glory by standing in the midst of the heavenly orders and delighting in the sight of God; so how does Satan stand thus to see God and enter into a dialogue with Him? Without doubt the standing here does not carry the literal meaning; rather, God permitted him the dialogue for the sake of divine justice and to confirm the freedom of rational creation, even in the case of Satan and his wicked hosts. Satan stood as though among the angels, being permitted to speak with God, but he did not enjoy the sight of God's glory, nor did the splendor of the divine glory shine upon him, nor did he experience the sweetness of God's voice as a source of delight, joy and true peace!

1.5.11.en: So on the great day of the Lord, the true believers will see in the eyes of Christ Jesus a gentle dove, and in His embrace inexpressible glories, but the wicked will see His eyes as a flame of fire, and will not bear to look at Him.

1.5.12.en: And just as it was said here of Satan that he stood presenting himself before God without enjoying the splendor of His glory, it was said in another place of the angels that they are "ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation" (Heb 1:14), but their being sent forth to serve does not deprive them of enjoying the divine presence and of the divine splendor shining upon them.

1.5.13.en: * Perhaps some will ask: How can Satan, who fell from his rank because of his pride, stand before the Lord among the angels?

1.5.14.en: Can he behold the Lord while he is unclean?

1.5.15.en: The devil and his hosts fell and it is no longer their right to see God, but according to his nature as a spirit he can present himself before God without beholding Him. So he stood complaining against us without seeing God, because he is unclean.

1.5.16.en: Note that it is said that he came before the Lord, and it is not said that he saw the Lord. For he came to be seen, not to see. He was before the eyes of the Lord, and the Lord was not before his eyes, just as a blind man stands before the sun: he himself is immersed in the rays of light, but he sees nothing of the radiant light... For the power of God, by its gaze, pierces all things, so it sees the unclean spirit that he does not see. For even the very things that flee from the face of God cannot be hidden, for all is naked before the eyes of the Most High. So the absent Satan came to Him who is present.

1.5.17.en: * Who are those called sons of God but the chosen angels? And as we know of them, they look upon the eyes of His majesty. It is fitting for us to ask: From where did they come to present themselves before God? For it was said of them by the voice of the Truth, "In heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven" (Mt 10:18). And the prophet says of them, "Thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him" (Dan 10:7). If they are always beholding and standing beside Him, we must carefully and exactly consider from where they came, for they never leave Him; but since Paul says of them, "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?" (Heb 14:1), from this we learn that they are sent, and we discover from where they came...

1.5.18.en: They do not go in a way that deprives them of the sight of God, so that the joys of inward contemplation are taken from them; for if by being sent they lost the vision of their Creator, they could not raise up the fallen, nor declare the truth to those in ignorance, and they could never offer to the blind what they were deprived of by leaving the source of light.

1.5.19.en: The nature of the angels differs from the state of our present nature, where we are bound by place and limited by the blindness of ignorance; but the spirits of the angels, though limited by place, have a knowledge that rises far above ours, beyond any comparison, a knowledge extending outwardly and inwardly, for they contemplate the very Source of knowledge itself...

1.5.20.en: And just as their spirits themselves, when compared with our bodies, are spirits, so when they are compared with the sublime, incomprehensible Spirit they are counted as body. Therefore they are sent from Him, and also stand before Him, for in this they are bound to be sent, and at the same time are wholly present and never leave Him.

1.5.21.en: So at the same time they always see the face of the Father, and yet they come to us, being sent through the quality of inward contemplation. It can then be said, "The sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord," as they return there by the return of the spirit, to where they never left Him by any withdrawal of the mind from Him.

1.5.23.en: "And the LORD said unto Satan, Whence comest thou?

1.6.0.en: Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it" [7].

1.6.1.en: By saying, "From going to and fro in the earth," he indicates that he did not exceed his limits, for "that great dragon... was cast out into the earth" (Rev 12:9). Many of the early Fathers of the Church see that the earth in the Holy Bible points to the earthly, carnal man who is occupied only with earthly things, so the enemy of good roams as in his own possession. Heaven, by contrast, points to the spiritual man, who is occupied with eternal things. Satan cannot creep into the heart of the spiritual man, but he roams without restraint in the heart of the carnal man.

1.6.2.en: The enemy of good knows no idleness, for he does not rest night or day from going to and fro in the earth to seduce the children of God to leave the kingdom of light and be occupied with sins.

1.6.3.en: * "From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it" [7]. You see that heaven is inaccessible to wicked Satan. If you say, "Well! Heaven is not open to him, but the world welcomes him." Yes, this is for your benefit, for if even with so vigilant an enemy you take no care to reform yourselves, what idle people you are...?

1.6.4.en: Listen to Paul as he says, "Whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme" (1 Tim 20:1).

1.6.5.en: Do you wish to hear another text? Do you not see the tormentors who accompany the officials? So Paul uses the demons. But the good results are not the work of Satan, but of God's love for man, who uses Satan for this purpose.

1.6.6.en: * What then does it mean that Satan is asked, "Whence comest thou?" but that He may condemn his ways as though they were unknown. For the light of the Truth knows nothing of the darkness, which it rebukes, nor of the ways of Satan, which it condemns as a judge. It is fitting that he be asked about them as though they were unknown. And for this reason it was said to Adam in his sin, by the voice of his Creator, "Adam... where art thou?" (Gen 9:3), for the divine power did not ignore the hidden place to which His servant had fled in his disobedience, but He saw that the one who fell in his sin was hiding from the eyes of the Truth under sin...

1.6.7.en: He condemns Satan; therefore his way was examined, but the chosen angels do not need to be asked from where they came, since their ways are known to God. They are, as it were, representing His movement, for they are subject to His will alone, and they cannot be unknown to Him.

1.6.8.en: * The devil roams on the earth, since he scorned to dwell in peace in the heights of heaven. And as one who is reported as not having flown but walked, he shows the weight of sin that keeps him always below...

1.6.9.en: God speaks with the angels when His inward will is disclosed to them as the object of their perception, while the angels speak with the Lord when by this they contemplate what is above them, and stand before Him in amazement. And so God speaks with the souls of His saints in one way, and they speak with Him in another... We see them in the Revelation: "They cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?... And it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season" (Rev 9:6-11).

1.6.10.en: God speaks with Satan in four ways: He condemns his unjust ways, He rebukes him by the righteousness of His saints, He permits him to test their innocence, and sometimes He stops him from tempting them...

1.7.0.en: He rebukes him by the righteousness of His chosen ones, when He says, "Hast thou considered my servant Job? for there is none like him in the earth (all)." He permitted him to put his righteousness to the test when He said to him, "Behold, all that he hath is in thy power" [12]. Again He prevented him from tempting him when He said, "Only upon himself put not forth thine hand" [12].

1.7.3.en: Hast thou considered my servant Job,

1.7.4.en: that there is none like him in the earth,

1.7.5.en: a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?" [8].

1.7.6.en: In God's speech with Satan He shows how much He esteems Job His servant, "for there is none like him in the earth" in uprightness and godliness. Through the relationship of mutual love between God and the true believer, the latter says, "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?" (Ex 15:11), "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage?" (Mic 7:18). And at the same time God esteems His believers in their faith, as with Job (Job 1:8), and the centurion, and the Canaanite woman, and the wonder is that all of them were Gentiles.

1.7.7.en: * Patience was indeed in Job, which God knew, and to which He bore witness, but it became known to men through the test of temptation. What was hidden within and unseen like fruit appeared by what happened and came to be outwardly.

1.7.8.en: St. Augustine * Satan resolved to enter into a struggle, not with Job but with God, while the blessed Job was the subject of dispute between them...

1.7.9.en: Had God not known that Job would certainly continue in his uprightness, He would not have delivered him to Satan. He did not deliver him to him in order to destroy him by the temptation... And the fires of envy were kindled in the mind of the tempter because of God's praise of him.

1.7.10.en: When the ancient enemy fails to discover any evil of which he can accuse us, he turns to the good points to turn them into evil, and when he is defeated in deeds he looks to our words to find room for accusation.

1.7.11.en: He struggles to darken the intention of the heart, so that our good works do not issue from a good mind, and thus are not considered good in the eyes of the Judge. For even if he sees fruit on a green tree in the heat, he looks for a worm to spoil the roots.

1.7.12.en: * Notice the stupidity and cunning of Satan. God bears witness that Job is blameless, so do you wish (O Satan) to snatch away the testimony of God...?

1.7.13.en: When God says, "My servant Job," this is sufficient to define his virtue...

1.7.14.en: He (Satan) was immediately enraged when he heard God call Job His servant, for to him this was counted as a rebuke of himself, and it provoked him to attack.

1.7.15.en: You (O Satan) were formerly a servant... This is what Paul meant: "Know ye not that we shall judge angels? how much more things that pertain to this life?" (1 Cor 3:6).

1.7.16.en: Job reached this degree so that God added: "A perfect and an upright man, (and true), one that feareth God." "An upright man," but you, on the contrary, though you are not a man, did not persevere in virtue.

1.7.17.en: St. John Chrysostom * [Hast thou considered my servant Job?] [8]. At the same time it precisely means that the traitor (the devil) bears a malicious intent toward those whom he counts as sinners because of their vices, and as righteous through his deception.

1.7.18.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem "Then Satan answered the LORD, and said,

1.7.19.en: Doth Job fear God for nought?" [9].

1.7.20.en: The enemy of good could not bear to hear a word of praise spoken of anyone other than himself, even though it came from God, who searches the hearts and knows the thoughts and all secrets. So King Saul could not bear the women praising the youth David, who had delivered him and all his army and his people from Goliath the giant and his army (1 Sam 18:6-9). And the chief priests and scribes could not bear the children praising the Lord Christ in the temple (Mt 21:15 etc.).

1.7.21.en: * Satan is called the slanderer because of his slanders, for he slanders man before God, saying, "Doth Job fear God for nought?"... and he slanders God before man, saying, "The fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep" (Job 16:1). He was eager to provoke him by saying that the calamity came down from heaven above, so as to set the servant at strife with the Master, and the Master with His servant. In fact he did not set them at strife, but he tried and was unable.

1.7.22.en: St. John Chrysostom * [He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor] (Ps 72:4). Rightly is Satan called the "slanderer" (the oppressor), for he slandered God, claiming that God forbade taking from the tree (of the knowledge of good and evil) out of envy, and he slandered Job with lies, saying [Doth Job really fear God for nought?... Put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face] (Job 1:9, 11). In the eighth Psalm He gave him two names, "the enemy and the avenger," while here (Ps 72:4) He calls him a slanderer.

1.7.23.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * Certainly Satan is the one who brings accusation against the saints. He cannot, in the presence of such a Judge, ascribe a false accusation, for he knows with whom he is speaking. Therefore, since he knows his inability to bring a false charge against us, he resorts to saying something true. Therefore our adversary, who envies us for being in the kingdom of heaven and does not want us to be there, from where he was cast out, says: [Doth Job serve God for nought?] (Job 1:9)...
